default.p.de-1-59.vietnamese:
I believe that a fairly large part of the causes behind the many misfortunes and anxieties people in today's world feel—whether consciously or, for the most part, unconsciously—are directly connected with the existence of what is called "the press." Or, perhaps more appropriately, one could say that it is modern culture itself—the culture that necessitates the existence of the press and supplies it with content—that is responsible for these things. Whatever the case may be, I still think that if every daily newspaper in the world were completely abolished, this world would become a slightly easier place to live. (Passage omitted)

The primary purpose of newspapers is to report as quickly as possible on events that occur each day. As an inevitable consequence, everyone knows that accuracy—the most important factor—tends to be sacrificed. However, even this one fact alone means that the influence of the press on the minds of people in modern times is by no means insignificant. Setting everything else aside, the unavoidable reality is that the press gradually erodes from everyone the attitude of "better late but certain," which is most essential for anyone seeking "truth." Of course, most people have an inclination toward purity when it comes to truth (fact), so inaccurate newspaper reports may happen to stimulate that desire for purity and, conversely, strongly encourage it to reemerge. Moreover, the vast majority of people already understand the "degree" of accuracy in newspaper reports, so they apply a certain safety factor before using the knowledge provided by the press; consequently, one might think that it causes no serious harm. If we are talking about the few excellent newspapers, that may in fact be true. However, the fundamental issue is why and to what extent "it is acceptable not to be accurate, as long as the information is obtained as quickly as possible" has become so important.

Some people may argue that the reason I say these things is ultimately that I have placed too much value on newspaper reports.

It is true that, in practice, many people may regard newspaper reports very lightly and pay them little attention. Yet is not the very habit of carelessly overlooking, morning and evening, events that are significant in every respect and should never be taken lightly a major cause of the defects in modern thinking? Is this habit not inadvertently leading us toward an irreversible decline?

default.p.de-1-63.vietnamese:
A

Today, email and messaging have become commonplace and brought us many conveniences. Compared with the past, we have entered an age in which we can exchange messages freely and quickly. However, can we really say that communication tools like these enable us to understand one another deeply? On the contrary, might they even cause misunderstandings because messages are incomplete?

The other day, a friend told me a story. They had received an email from a close friend with whom they had just argued over something trivial. The email said, “Let’s end this.” My friend said they had agonized over whether it meant, “Let’s end the argument and make up,” or, “Let’s end our friendship from this point on.”

Email is certainly fast and convenient. However, I think that if we use this as a reason to neglect direct communication—meeting and talking with one another—then it defeats the whole purpose.

B

I believe that in a society overflowing with information, what we need is the ability to select the information we need and the ability to judge whether information is reliable. Without these two abilities, would we not simply be swept along by the flow of information?

I myself once had a failed experience when I was a first-year student. For a summer independent research assignment, I prepared and submitted a report on the topic “Endangered Wildlife.” However, my teacher pointed out that there was still a question as to whether the content on the Internet homepage I had consulted was reliable. I immediately checked the website again. It turned out that some pages had not been updated even once in five years, while others dealt only with a specific local area of the world.

Accepting information without thinking is extremely dangerous. Rather than swallowing information whole—accepting it blindly—we must select what is truly necessary and have the ability to judge it accurately. That is what each of us is now required to do.

default.p.de-1-66.vietnamese:
The most ordinary appeal of what is called a novel lies in making readers forget themselves. They forget who they are, become characters in the novel, and imagine that they are living the lives depicted in it. The pleasure of imagining that one is falling in love or committing murder alongside the characters, and surrendering oneself to that pleasure, is the most ordinary attraction of a novel. Of course, this is a fundamental appeal of the novel, and something without this appeal could hardly be called a novel in the first place. However, ordinary readers do not seek any appeal beyond this basic attraction. They make no effort to take even one step beyond the way a child reads adventure stories with their ears covered.

In Hudson's book Naturalist in La Plata, there is a story about foxes and their instinct to feign death. When danger approaches, a fox pretends to be dead. From time to time, it slightly opens one eye to check whether it is safe. Once it realizes that the danger has passed, it slowly gets up and runs away. This tactic is said to be so extremely ingenious that dogs are completely deceived. Yet there is also a story that the tactic was so ingenious that the fox actually died: when someone conducted an experiment, the fox continued pretending to be dead until its body was cut apart. (Middle section omitted.)

There is no need to try anything in reality, because reading novels gives people the feeling that they are doing everything in real life, and in the end they do nothing in the real world. They remain sitting in one place, enjoying the illusion that they have experienced life and letting time pass. For example, even if they have never been in love in reality, they skim through all kinds of wonderful love stories in novels. Once they have absorbed the technique of pretending to be in love, they no longer understand what genuine love really is. Even if they find a real romantic partner, it is not easy to discard this technique of pretending to love, to the point that, when they look at themselves, they cannot even tell whether they are in a novel or genuinely in love in real life.

People fall into this condition because they have never seriously considered how to read novels. They merely receive novels as a kind of stimulation that makes them lose themselves. As a result, they gradually become addicted.

This applies not only to novels but also to various kinds of books on ideas. Reading is not a matter of leaving one's mind completely empty so that the other side can fill it. Reading is also a genuine experience, just like an experience in real life. Unless the reader's mind remains constantly alert and engages in dialogue with and confronts the page, the reader will gain nothing from the book, just as one gains nothing from an experience in real life without truly taking it in. In that sense, the novelist is not the only creator of a novel. Through reading, the reader also contributes, through their own abilities, to the work created by the writer. This awareness of collaboration is the true pleasure of reading, and I believe we should make an effort to discover how to read in order to achieve that pleasure. The same applies to learning ideas from books: we should reflect on ourselves in order to understand the ideas that have been written, rather than allowing those ideas to make us lose ourselves. I believe that, just as reading romantic novels and losing oneself while learning someone else's technique of pretending to love is unacceptable, learning someone else's technique of pretending to think is also unacceptable.

(From “On Reading” by Kobayashi Hideo)

We hope this letter finds your company in good health and continued prosperity. We sincerely thank you for your continued special favor and support.

Regarding the product 〇〇〇 that your company recently ordered, we would like to apologize and make a request.

Unfortunately, we received more orders from throughout the country than expected, resulting in an unforeseen delay in production.

default.p.de-1-50.vietnamese:
People once used to say that the moment when an actor suddenly stumbled on stage—misspeaking or making a slip of the tongue—was when theater demonstrated its greatest expressive power. This view is not entirely foolish or unreasonable. At that very moment, theater briefly intersected with the “non-theatrical,” and the theatrical mechanism itself was objectified, becoming something to be examined.

Of course, in an era when “theater” or “performance” maintained a firm distance from the non-theatrical—that is, what is called “real life”—in order to preserve a stable, symmetrical tension, nothing of the sort occurred. “Theater” was then tested only by its ability to take flight from the firm and stable ground called “real life,” and an actor's stumble on stage was merely evidence of that failed takeoff—the loss of speed and fall back down.

However, when the foundation of what was called “the real” in “real life” began to be questioned, the situation changed profoundly. If “real life,” which had been the premise for testing theater's ability to take flight, lost its stability, then naturally neither “theater” nor “real life” could retain the position of being the subject with the other as subordinate. All that remained was the relationship that “this is not that, and that is not this.” The healthy tension that had once existed between “theater” and “real life” disappeared, and the two began confronting each other directly and doubting one another.

It is often thought that the realist method of modern theater was developed to rely on a firm sense of “real life” in order to question “theater.” More accurately, however, because we had lost a firm sense of “real life,” the method was created to objectify real life through “theater.” In other words, it was a method of using “theater” to question “real life.” The issue, of course, is not realism itself. The essential issue is the transformation in the relationship between “theater” and “real life”: the introduction of this method caused “theater” to question “real life,” while “real life” could not help questioning “theater” in turn.

(From Minoru Betsuyaku, 『言葉への戦術』)

(Note 1) トチル: For an actor to make a mistake on stage, such as getting a line or gesture wrong. (Note 2) あながち: Not something that can be stated categorically or one-sidedly. (Note 3) 写実主義 = realism: Depicting reality as it is, without beautifying it.

default.p.de-1-53.vietnamese:
“To know” means perceiving and thinking about things that exist. In other words, we cannot know about things that do not exist. “To know” means that something is present there. When we do not know what something is, we lose a clue for action and become uneasy. Then, when we say that we know something, how much do we actually know about it? (Middle section omitted)

We cannot know things that exist in an absolute and comprehensive way. We perceive things through our own senses and reason. In other words, our knowledge operates within the framework of our body and mind. Conversely, it is precisely because we perceive and think about reality through these means that we become separated from reality itself. Knowledge is established through mediation. That is, ( ① ).

We cannot know things exactly as they are in themselves. Perhaps eyes different from human eyes would see a scene different from the one reflected in human eyes. For example, the green world, which has great significance in human color experience, is presumed to appear light gray to insects. A brain different from the human brain would surely produce different thoughts. A mind that does not regard accuracy and rigor as its only ideals might give birth to a different mathematics and a different physics from those that currently exist. Without even considering robots, even scientific knowledge cannot be completely objective knowledge.

More precisely, if truth is defined as correspondence with existing reality, knowledge and truth are entirely different things. ( ② ), knowledge that is completely detached from truth cannot be called knowledge. It is merely an error or an illusion. No knowledge can be absolute, but even so, knowledge is neither religious belief nor subjective opinion.

default.p.de-1-56.vietnamese:
That morning, before going to school, Kimiko’s older brother Masao suddenly flung open the sliding door to her room and poked in his usually expressionless face. “Hey, I hear your fever still hasn’t gone down?”

He was a junior high school student, five years older than Kimiko. Normally, he was distant and cold about everything, giving the impression that he was saying, “I couldn’t care less about a little sister like you.” Although they were the only two siblings, perhaps because of their considerable age difference, Kimiko could not remember ever playing with him. Kimiko, a third-grade elementary school girl, did not particularly like such a brother. Unlike her father, he seemed to her like a strange man from outside the family.

Masao entered the room and squatted down beside the pillow where Kimiko lay sleeping. “Don’t go and give me the flu, okay? ...I’ve got an entrance examination coming up,” he said curtly. Kimiko thought to herself, “If you don’t want to catch it, wouldn’t it be better if you didn’t come in here?”

Since the previous night, her fever had remained around 38°C. Her head felt unbearably heavy, and she was miserable and restless. At that point, even breathing in and out was exhausting. Thinking that she must not pass her cold and flu on to her brother, Kimiko pulled the quilt up over her mouth and nose.

The official entrance examination was only a few days away. If he caught the flu now, the consequences would be disastrous. Three years of hard study could all go to waste.

“Kimiko, how many faces have you found?” Masao, still squatting beside her pillow, suddenly looked up at the ceiling and asked. “There are nine faces in this room.” He pointed to one corner of the ceiling.

Kimiko followed his direction with her dull, heavy eyes. Sure enough, there was something that looked like a human face. The five-year-old wood grain on the ceiling board looked like the profile of a face, with a protruding chin.

“See? Right? That makes one. Find the other eight yourself.” Masao stood up decisively, left her with those words, and walked out of the room. (Passage omitted)

As the sun gradually set, the ceiling began to darken from the corners. Just as Kimiko thought it was impossible to continue searching, the sliding door suddenly flew open. “Hey, Kimiko. Have you found them all?” Masao stood there with the same unchanging cold expression as always.

Kimiko smiled and shook her head. “I can’t find just one more.” “Hmm... I suppose that’s true.” Masao pressed the switch on the wall. The ceiling light came on, brightly illuminating the entire room.

“Look over there, at that corner. Isn’t that one?” Near the top of the wall, a faint shadow appeared. A random indentation caused by some impact, highlighted by the light bulb, stood out like the profile of a human face.

“So that’s what it was.” ① Kimiko felt as if she had been tricked, but strangely, she was not angry at all. On the contrary, she felt happier and more excited than ever.

“Big brother. My fever’s gone down.” Kimiko smiled at him from her bed.

Masao rarely smiled, but immediately covered his nose and mouth tightly with both hands and said: ② “Dangerous, very dangerous. The flu is most contagious just when you’re about to recover.” As he said this, he walked out of the room.

(Adapted from Ryuichiro Utsumi’s work “Faces on the Ceiling”)

default.p.de-2-59.vietnamese:
People often talk about whether someone is cultured or uncultured. Let us set aside for the moment the question of what exactly someone possesses when we say they are "cultured," and first consider the matter from the perspective of being "uncultured."

When we say that someone is "uncultured," the word "not" does not seem to mean "not possessing anything at all"—being completely empty. For example, people do not usually say, "That guy has absolutely no culture whatsoever," in the same sense as saying, "There is not even a single coin in his wallet." Saying that someone is "uncultured" means not merely that they lack culture, but that something different from culture—or something completely opposed to it—is present instead. That is precisely why being "uncultured" is genuinely troublesome and bothersome.

First, let us consider an uncultured human being. Take, for example, a one- or two-year-old infant. No matter how intelligent or quick to understand things that one- or two-year-old may be, no one would ever say, "That child has a rich culture." This is because infants naturally live according to biological needs and simple emotions such as anger and sadness. (Passage omitted.) Therefore, being "uncultured" does not mean lacking something; it means living solely according to biological desires, sudden impulses, and extremely primitive emotions.

To explain it more clearly: someone who craves whatever they want to the point of being unable to restrain themselves, or who, whenever angry, gives free rein to that impulse and screams wildly without regard for those around them—such a person cannot be called cultured, no matter how much they may know. Earlier I used the phrase "no matter how much they may know," but being cultured and knowing many things are completely different. Not everyone who knows a great deal is cultured. In a life filled with many different specialized things and surrounded by them, it is entirely unrealistic to expect oneself to know everything in the world thoroughly.

(From Hori Hidehiko's "Living Fully Through High School")

(Note 1) Mōtō (毛頭): not even a little, in the slightest.
(Note 2) Yamo tatemo tamaranai (矢も楯もたまらない): an emotion that cannot be restrained no matter what.

default.p.de-2-63.vietnamese:
A

The first outsiders a child encounters are their parents. The child is influenced by them, imitates them, and grows up. If a child has distorted experiences during childhood in an unsuitable environment, this will certainly leave some negative influence after they grow up. Early education may help children become skilled at thinking about things logically, but it may also prevent them from developing the emotions needed to perceive things from an emotional perspective. If children naturally interact and play with adults and peers while gradually accumulating a wide variety of experiences, they can develop a balance between intellect and emotion on their own. But in an environment such as enrichment classes, isn't that balance likely to be disrupted? (A section is omitted.)

Both parents and education researchers seem to be struggling with the question of whether children should receive early education. Wouldn't increasing the number of classes where children can experience enrichment learning as play help ease the conflict and concerns troubling parents?

B

Before and after enrolling a child in early education, the amount of time spent with the child differs greatly. There are reportedly studies showing that early education increases the amount of time parents actively engage with their children, leading to more close physical contact (“skinship”) and a deeper parent-child relationship.

On the other hand, the early education being promoted today is also a typical example of a highly modern, management-oriented approach to child-rearing. Early education controls young children's sight and hearing while creating the illusion that they are choosing learning materials with “intentions” that adults have already designed, and it makes them respond obediently and submissively. It tries to separate out and “stuff” children with visible, tangible abilities such as “being able to speak” and “understanding numbers,” while neglecting the invisible process of “maturing emotionally.” The “concept of ability” envisioned by early education completely lacks a “concept of the human being.” We must recognize that this is both the key to the success of the early education system currently being implemented and, at the same time, an enormous trap.

(Note 1) 葛藤: Inner conflict and turmoil
(Note 2) スキンシップ: A child-rearing method in which parents and children make physical contact to build an emotional bond.

default.p.de-2-66.vietnamese:
If asked what music is, I usually answer that it is a conversation through sound. Through sound, one person's emotions and ideas are conveyed to the listener. That is music.

Such a definition seems self-evident, but music is not always like that. Simply put, whether happy or sad, we sometimes sing alone. It is not to have anyone listen. Our emotions simply flow away on their own. There is no one there to converse with.

If we consider such songs to be self-talk and therefore a kind of dialogue, what about hymns sung in temples or churches? Of course, they are certainly directed toward God, but the word 'dialogue' is not entirely appropriate. In particular, in indigenous folk religions, it is difficult to call music that brings people into an intense ecstatic state a dialogue. The sound of a battle trumpet or hunting drum is the same: because it conveys meaning in only one direction, it is not a genuine conversation.

There is no doubt that the kinds of music mentioned above are also music. Therefore, my definition is not really a good definition at all; it is merely the wish and image of music that I myself hold.

Once something is a dialogue, it differs from stimulation or pleasure delivered in a one-way manner. At a concert, the performers are musicians and we simply listen in silence, but that absolutely does not mean that we passively receive the sounds. If we listen to sounds in a vague, unfocused way, music becomes nothing more than a chain of connected sounds. To hear it as a musical work, the listener must in fact engage in considerable mental activity as well.

What I still remember vividly is a passage from a diary written by the novelist Takami Jun shortly before his death. He wrote that his body had become so weak that he no longer had the strength to read, and he thought music might still be possible, so he tried listening to it—but it did not work. He could naturally hear the sounds, but he could not hear them as music. This was not a decline in hearing, but a deterioration of the mental ability to reconstruct what the ears received into meaningful words within himself.

Not only music but the appreciation of art itself is an attempt to reach another person's world. It can also be described as understanding others through sound, color, or words. Leaving aside the question of whether people can ultimately understand one another, I believe it is fair to say that the meaning of art itself lies in the effort to try to understand.

(Excerpt from "The Music of Dialogue" by Toyama Kazuyuki)

(Note) Ecstasy: A state of intense emotional exaltation in which one forgets oneself.

Dear Members of the Association,

As the year draws to a close, we sincerely wish your association continued prosperity. We would also like to express our heartfelt gratitude for the exceptional guidance and support you have given us over the years.

Thank you very much for inviting us to this year’s “New Year’s Welcome Gathering.” We tried our best to arrange our schedules so that we could attend, but unfortunately, both our president and managing director must travel abroad on that day and are unable to change their schedules in the country they are visiting. Although we are deeply sorry to decline your kind invitation, we respectfully ask for your understanding and forgiveness for the absence of both executives.

In addition, if your association permits a substitute attendee, we would be happy to send a member of our company’s executive committee. Please let us know if this would be acceptable.

We look forward to receiving your continued guidance in the future.

Sincerely,

default.p.de-2-50.vietnamese:
What is the other person thinking as we communicate with them, what are they paying attention to, and what do they know or not know? The essence of communication is deliberately changing that person’s inner world, known as their cognitive environment. This view is completely opposed to the idea that communication is the transmission of “meaning” through words. Let us examine the following two examples.

Case 1: A: “Would you like some coffee?” — B: “Coffee really does wake you up, doesn’t it?”
Case 2: A: “What are you planning to do today?” — B: “I have a terrible headache.”

What does B’s statement in Case 1 imply? Clearly, B is not merely communicating the fact that “coffee helps you stay alert” to A. If B is about to go to sleep, the statement means “I don’t need coffee,” whereas if B is preparing to work through the night, it means “I’d like a cup, please.”

What about Case 2? In response to the question “What are you planning to do today?”, B does not answer what they will do today, nor do they say that they will do nothing. Instead, for some reason, B merely tells the other person the fact that “I have a headache.”

Case 1 is a type of communication in which the intention can easily be reduced to one specific interpretation. The result of the exchange is directly tied to the action of accepting or declining the coffee. In contrast, in Case 2, the exchange contains no clear message that obligates either A or B to take a particular action. It is not at all clear what B wants A to do by saying “I have a terrible headache.” What matters, however, is that B’s words in Case 2 dramatically changed A’s cognitive environment. This dramatic change may not compel A to take any specific action. Nevertheless, A has begun thinking about things that had never occurred to them before hearing B’s words. If this is not communication, then what is?

(From Understanding Other People’s Minds by Kanazawa So)

default.p.de-2-53.vietnamese:
In Japan, the word “leisure” seems to be received with a certain sense of tension and hostility. Why do people not use the old word “hima,” meaning free time? The deliberate replacement of “hima” with the foreign word “leisure” itself shows that the thing no longer has any sense of ease or leisure.

“Leisure” is completely different from what is called “hima.” “Leisure” is calculated and allocated, but it must eventually be consumed. Through leisure activities, people are forced to restore their energy so that they can continue working. Am I the only one who feels as if I am being forced to engage in leisure activities as though following an imperative?

I think “hima” is a period when we do nothing. If stating it so definitively seems somewhat extreme, we could put it this way: whatever we may do, it is a period when we are free to take the initiative and do what we like on our own. Of course, this also includes doing nothing and simply being idle and relaxed.

Even so, it is not right to think of free time as an empty period. On the contrary, precisely because it is a time of ease, we are living more fully and completely than when we are working—we can sense the subtle stirrings of life that we cannot perceive when we are busy, and devote our entire minds and bodies to receiving the joy of being alive. At least, that is how I see it.

In general, I cannot understand why human life should be sharply divided into two separate halves: working time and free time.

Work is boring, work is difficult, but leisure is fun, and leisure is the purpose of life—that people are forced to make such a sharp distinction is, I think, a clear indication of the weakness of modern machine-based civilization.

(From Tanikawa Shuntaro's “26 Lectures on the Alphabet”)

default.p.de-2-56.outline.0.label: Changes in the relationship between close friends
default.p.de-2-56.outline.0.note: Compares close friends in the past, who openly expressed their true feelings, with close friends today, who suppress emotions to maintain good relationships
default.p.de-2-56.outline.1.label: Indifference in public places caused by psychological exhaustion
default.p.de-2-56.outline.1.note: Carefree behavior in public and indifference to those around them reflect the fact that they have devoted all their energy to intimate relationships.
default.p.de-2-56.outline.2.label: Fear of conflict and the emergence of “gentle relationships”
default.p.de-2-56.outline.2.note: Intimate relationships are as fragile as glass; exposing points of opposition is a major threat, so gentle relationship techniques are necessary.
default.p.de-2-56.outline.3.label: Using ambiguous expressions to avoid opposition
default.p.de-2-56.outline.3.note: Young people create ambiguous expressions (ぼかし表現) to blur disagreements and maintain a safe distance.
default.p.de-2-56.vietnamese:
If a close friend used to be someone with whom people could openly express their honest feelings, a close friend today has instead become someone from whom people feel they must hold those feelings back.

This is because they feel that otherwise it would be difficult to maintain a good relationship with the other person.

On the other hand, people who behave according to their instinctive desires in public spaces such as trains—for example, high school students enthusiastically absorbed in talking on their mobile phones, or young women who change out of their school uniforms and put on makeup—seem to push everyone else present outside their world. Even when they notice them, the others appear merely as part of the surrounding scenery, not as meaningful individuals. If so, could the truth be the reverse: that their complete indifference to third parties in public spaces, and their failure to perceive others as meaningful individuals, is a sign that they have exhausted all their energy within their intimate relationships?

For children today, relationships with others within their intimate sphere seem to be an excessively heavy burden. For those who manage their relationships with others as carefully as if they were handling fragile glass, exposing their mutual differences must feel like an unbearable threat.

As a result, such an abnormal situation becomes something that must be avoided at all costs. In response, techniques for creating “gentle relationships,” in which differences are not exposed, have spread in an extremely subtle form.

Among young people, rather than focusing on each other's differences and points of opposition in order to resolve them, many “gentle techniques” have been created that pretend such opposition does not exist. Expressions that are vague and avoid making definite statements, such as “Why don't we go get something to eat for now?” and “As for me, I've decided on this,” are examples of such techniques. They frequently use these expressions in everyday life to avoid conflict with others. By blurring their own statements, they make differences invisible and try to maintain a subtle distance from the other person. Since this is not a matter of yielding after carefully considering the other person's position or opinion, these “vague expressions” are used thoroughly even though honorific language is scarcely used.

（Based on Takayoshi Doi's book *Children Driven by Individualism*）

（Note）マネージメント (Management): In this passage, treating relationships between people with care. おもんぱかって (Omonpakatte): carefully considering all circumstances and their effects.
